title: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE
subtitle: Writing data — add, modify, and remove rows
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: SQL isn't just for reading data — you need to add new records, update existing ones, and remove old ones.
whyItExists.solution: INSERT adds rows. UPDATE changes existing rows. DELETE removes rows. All support WHERE clauses. All should be used inside transactions for safety.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Whenever your application needs to write data: user registration (INSERT), profile update (UPDATE), account deletion (DELETE).
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Never run UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE clause in production — it affects every row. Always test with SELECT first.

explainModes.beginner: INSERT adds a new row. UPDATE changes values in existing rows — always add WHERE or it changes EVERY row. DELETE removes rows — again, always add WHERE or it deletes EVERYTHING.
explainModes.simple: INSERT INTO table (col1, col2) VALUES (val1, val2). Multiple rows: VALUES (v1,v2),(v3,v4). INSERT OR REPLACE / ON CONFLICT (upsert). UPDATE table SET col=val WHERE condition. DELETE FROM table WHERE condition. TRUNCATE TABLE (not SQLite) — fast delete all rows. INSERT INTO table SELECT ... — insert from query.
explainModes.standard: Always use transactions for related writes (INSERT + UPDATE together). UPDATE without WHERE = update all rows — very dangerous. DELETE without WHERE = delete all rows. RETURNING clause (PostgreSQL, SQLite 3.35+) returns affected rows — useful for getting auto-generated IDs. INSERT OR IGNORE (SQLite) silently ignores rows that violate constraints. ON CONFLICT (col) DO UPDATE SET ... (standard upsert).
explainModes.technical: AUTOINCREMENT (SQLite) / SERIAL / GENERATED AS IDENTITY (PostgreSQL) for auto-generated primary keys. Bulk INSERT with multiple value rows is much faster than individual INSERTs (fewer round-trips). COPY command (PostgreSQL) for bulk loading from files — fastest option. INSERT INTO ... SELECT ... for moving/copying data between tables. RETURNING *  gives the inserted/updated row back without a second query.
explainModes.deepDive: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL): writes go to the WAL file first, then are checkpointed to the main database. This provides crash recovery. MVCC: UPDATE is internally DELETE + INSERT of a new version — old versions are vacuumed later (PostgreSQL VACUUM). SQLite's rowid is a hidden 64-bit integer key for all tables without an explicit INTEGER PRIMARY KEY. Conflict resolution in SQLite: OR IGNORE, OR REPLACE, OR FAIL, OR ABORT, OR ROLLBACK. PostgreSQL's ON CONFLICT is SQL-standard MERGE-lite.

content.code:
-- Insert a single row
INSERT INTO users (name, email, city, joined_at)
VALUES ('New User', 'new@example.com', 'Pune', '2024-07-01');

-- Insert multiple rows at once
INSERT INTO products (name, category, price, stock)
VALUES
    ('JavaScript Handbook', 'Books', 449, 300),
    ('Ergonomic Mouse', 'Electronics', 1499, 60),
    ('USB Hub', 'Electronics', 899, 90);

-- Insert from a SELECT query
-- (duplicate all book products to an archive table)
-- INSERT INTO archive_products
-- SELECT * FROM products WHERE category = 'Books';

-- Upsert: insert or update on conflict (SQLite)
INSERT INTO users (id, name, email, city, joined_at)
VALUES (1, 'Prashant Updated', 'p2@example.com', 'Delhi', '2024-01-15')
ON CONFLICT(id) DO UPDATE SET
    name = excluded.name,
    email = excluded.email;

-- UPDATE: change specific rows
-- ALWAYS include WHERE unless you want to update ALL rows!
UPDATE products
SET price = 549, stock = 120
WHERE id = 1;

-- Update multiple columns
UPDATE users
SET city = 'Hyderabad', email = 'updated@example.com'
WHERE id = 3;

-- Update based on a calculation
UPDATE products
SET price = ROUND(price * 1.10, 2)  -- 10% price increase
WHERE category = 'Books';

-- DELETE: remove specific rows
-- ALWAYS include WHERE!
DELETE FROM orders WHERE id = 8;

-- Delete based on a join condition (using a subquery)
DELETE FROM orders
WHERE user_id = (SELECT id FROM users WHERE email = 'bob@example.com');

-- Check before deleting: run SELECT first!
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 3;  -- verify
-- Then: DELETE FROM orders WHERE user_id = 3;

content.text: UPDATE and DELETE without a WHERE clause affect ALL rows. Before running either command in production, always run SELECT with the same WHERE condition first to preview affected rows. Wrap destructive operations in a transaction so you can ROLLBACK if something is wrong.

questions.question: What happens if you run UPDATE products SET price = 999 without a WHERE clause?
options: An error is raised — WHERE is required
Only the first row is updated
Every row in the products table gets price = 999
questions.explanation: Without WHERE, UPDATE applies to every row in the table. This is almost always a bug. Always run SELECT with the same WHERE condition first to preview what will be updated, then use a transaction so you can ROLLBACK if needed.

faq.q: How do I get the auto-generated ID after INSERT?
faq.a: In SQLite: SELECT last_insert_rowid() immediately after INSERT. In PostgreSQL: INSERT INTO table (...) VALUES (...) RETURNING id. In most database drivers (Python's sqlite3, Node's better-sqlite3), the lastInsertRowid is returned directly from the execute call.

examples: INSERT INTO users (name, email, hashed_password) VALUES (?, ?, ?) — user signup
UPDATE users SET last_login = NOW() WHERE id = ? — track login time
UPDATE posts SET deleted_at = NOW() WHERE id = ? — soft delete (don't actually delete)
